title: Testing the argument-stability condition from prover-estimator debate in a toy debate
quick_reasoning: Directly tests a formal scalable-oversight (debate) safety condition with a focused empirical harness.

original_idea.body:
# Testing the argument-stability condition from prover-estimator debate in a toy debate

**Problem:** Prover-Estimator Debate (2025-2026) proves that an 'argument stability' condition lets debate avoid the obfuscated-arguments problem. The formal condition has not been illustrated empirically on a small, human-judgeable task.

**Direction:** Build a tiny debate harness: two open instruct models argue over a verifiable claim (e.g. a multi-step arithmetic or factual decomposition), with a third weak model as estimator. Construct cases that are 'stable' vs deliberately 'unstable' (small perturbations flip the sub-claim) and measure whether the honest side wins more often in stable cases. Success = a win-rate comparison aligning with the stability prediction.

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight via debate is a key non-lab safety bet. An accessible empirical illustration of when debate's guarantees hold helps the community calibrate expectations using only open models.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate' (arXiv:2506.13609, 2025-2026), which introduces the formal argument-stability condition.

title: When does debate help a weak judge? Replicating knowledge-divergence predictions
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped study of scalable-oversight debate value, a core AI safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# When does debate help a weak judge? Replicating knowledge-divergence predictions

**Problem:** 'Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight' (2026) argues debate's value depends on the knowledge gap between debaters and judge. The quantitative relationship between divergence and judge accuracy gain is not well mapped on open models.

**Direction:** Use an open weak judge model and open stronger debater models on a QA task. Systematically vary the capability gap (use models of different sizes) and measure judge accuracy with debate vs without (consultancy/single-answer baseline). Plot accuracy gain vs measured knowledge divergence. Success = a curve relating divergence to debate's benefit.

**Why it matters:** Tells practitioners outside labs when cheap debate-based oversight actually buys safety and when it doesn't — a directly usable design guideline produced with inference-only open models.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight' (arXiv:2603.05293, 2026).

title: Can a weak judge be tricked into rewarding a stronger model? A small-scale audit
quick_reasoning: Maps failure boundary of weak-judge scalable oversight, a well-defined safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Can a weak judge be tricked into rewarding a stronger model? A small-scale audit

**Problem:** 'Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models' (2026) shows debate can let weak judges correctly reward stronger models — but the failure boundary (when weak judges are instead manipulated) is under-characterized.

**Direction:** Reproduce a minimal version with an open weak judge and stronger open debaters, then adversarially craft persuasive-but-wrong arguments and measure how often the weak judge is fooled vs correctly defers. Map the boundary by topic difficulty. Success = a fooled-rate table identifying conditions where weak-judge debate breaks.

**Why it matters:** Weak-judge oversight is the most resource-light scalable-oversight path. Knowing where it fails is safety-critical and trivially doable outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models' (arXiv:2605.27483, 2026).

title: Probing MechELK latent-knowledge elicitation on a small open 'quirky' model
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses ELK, a core AI safety problem, with a focused model-organism probe.

original_idea.body:
# Probing MechELK latent-knowledge elicitation on a small open 'quirky' model

**Problem:** MechELK (April 2026) proposes a three-stage mechanistic framework to elicit latent knowledge LLMs hold but don't output. Its stages have not been independently validated on a small, controllable model organism.

**Direction:** Use the existing open 'Quirky'/Taboo-style models (publicly released) where the model knows but hides a fact. Apply lightweight elicitation probes (logit lens, simple linear probes on hidden states — no SAE training) inspired by MechELK's pipeline and measure recovery rate of the hidden fact vs the model's stated answer. Success = elicitation accuracy curves on a held-out fact set.

**Why it matters:** ELK is a core ARC open problem and a long-horizon safety bet. Probing existing open model organisms needs no training and is exactly the kind of model-organism study favored for counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'MechELK: A Mechanistic Interpretability Framework for Eliciting Latent Knowledge in LLMs' (arXiv:2605.28825, April 2026) and uses the 'Quirky' models from arXiv:2312.01037.

title: Logit-lens vs SAE for ELK: a cheap apples-to-apples comparison
quick_reasoning: Focused comparison of ELK elicitation methods, a recognized safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Logit-lens vs SAE for ELK: a cheap apples-to-apples comparison

**Problem:** 'Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability' (May 2025) used both logit lens and sparse autoencoders on a Taboo model. Which method better recovers hidden knowledge under a tight compute budget is unclear.

**Direction:** On the released Taboo model, compare an inference-only logit-lens elicitation against using a PRE-TRAINED open SAE (no SAE training) for the same model layer. Measure hidden-word recovery accuracy and compute cost. Success = a head-to-head table with a recommendation under the 'consumer GPU' constraint.

**Why it matters:** Gives beginners and small labs a concrete, budget-aware recipe for the cheapest reliable ELK probe — practical safety tooling that needs no proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability' (arXiv:2505.14352, May 2025), reusing its Taboo model setup.

title: Reproducing the geometric-inductive-bias account of grokking on modular arithmetic
quick_reasoning: Inductive bias/generalization bears on goal misgeneralization; safety link reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducing the geometric-inductive-bias account of grokking on modular arithmetic

**Problem:** A March 2026 paper argues grokking (delayed generalization) is driven by excess architectural degrees of freedom — unconstrained representational magnitude and data-dependent attention routing. The claim deserves independent replication on the canonical modular-arithmetic task.

**Direction:** Train a tiny transformer (fits on a single GPU in minutes) on modular addition — this is small-scale, not 'training from scratch' at frontier scale. Toggle the architectural constraints the paper identifies (weight norm caps, attention routing) and measure whether grokking onset shifts as predicted. Note: this is the one borderline-training idea; kept because the model is toy-sized and the experiment is the point. Success = grokking-time curves under each architectural intervention.

**Why it matters:** Inductive bias is an Open-Phil-listed alignment open problem: understanding what generalization a network 'prefers' bears on goal misgeneralization. A clean replication clarifies a mechanistic claim with only toy compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Geometric Inductive Bias of Grokking: Bypassing Phase Transitions via Architectural Topology' (arXiv:2603.05228, 2026), which has public code on GitHub (AlperYildirim1/geometric-grokking).

title: Does the local learning coefficient predict grokking difficulty? A small SLT probe
quick_reasoning: SLT probe of capability phase transitions, relevant to predicting emergent dangerous capabilities.

original_idea.body:
# Does the local learning coefficient predict grokking difficulty? A small SLT probe

**Problem:** A 2026 singular-learning-theory paper tests an Arrhenius-style hypothesis that the local learning coefficient (LLC) scales with problem difficulty in a grokking modular-arithmetic model. The relationship needs independent checks across moduli.

**Direction:** Using an existing open LLC estimator (devinterp library) and a toy modular-arithmetic transformer, measure how the estimated LLC varies with task difficulty (modulus size, number of operations) and test whether it tracks grokking time as the SLT paper predicts. Success = a scatter of LLC vs grokking onset with a fitted trend.

**Why it matters:** SLT promises a principled, training-free-at-inference geometric probe of when a network undergoes capability phase transitions — relevant to predicting emergent dangerous capabilities. Reproducible on toy models with open tooling.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Using physics-inspired Singular Learning Theory to understand grokking & other phase transitions' (arXiv:2512.00686, Dec 2025) and the basin-selection SLT view (arXiv:2603.01192, 2026); uses the open devinterp library.

title: Applying the Loss Kernel geometric probe to a small safety-relevant classifier
quick_reasoning: Anomaly/backdoor detection via geometric probe maps to a recognized interpretability safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Applying the Loss Kernel geometric probe to a small safety-relevant classifier

**Problem:** 'The Loss Kernel: A Geometric Probe for Deep Learning Interpretability' (2025) proposes a geometric probe of model behavior, but it has not been applied to detect anomalous behavior on a model with a known backdoor/anomalous mode.

**Direction:** Take a small open model or train a tiny classifier with a deliberately inserted spurious feature (toy backdoor). Apply the Loss Kernel probe (using authors' described method) and test whether the geometric signal distinguishes clean inputs from inputs triggering the anomalous mode. Success = an AUROC for anomaly detection via the kernel signal.

**Why it matters:** ARC's open problem of 'formal mechanistic explanations for anomalous behavior on novel inputs' maps directly here. A cheap geometric anomaly detector usable on open models is valuable independent safety tooling.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Loss Kernel: A Geometric Probe for Deep Learning Interpretability' (arXiv:2509.26537, 2025).

title: Replicating SAE 'concept crystals' geometry on a fresh open SAE
quick_reasoning: Tests whether interpretability-based safety claims generalize; safety relevance immediate.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating SAE 'concept crystals' geometry on a fresh open SAE

**Problem:** 'The Geometry of Concepts' showed SAE feature dictionaries contain 'crystal' structures (parallelograms generalizing king:queen::man:woman). Whether this geometry replicates on newer open SAEs released for different models is open.

**Direction:** Download a publicly released SAE for an open LLM (no SAE training), extract feature vectors, and search for parallelogram/trapezoid 'crystals' using the paper's described linear-algebra tests (after projecting out distractor dimensions). Quantify how many clean analogy crystals appear vs a random-vector baseline. Success = a count of validated crystals with a statistical significance test against the baseline.

**Why it matters:** Whether interpretable features have stable geometric structure bears on whether interpretability-based safety claims generalize. A replication on a new SAE is pure linear algebra plus inference — ideal for beginners and counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Geometry of Concepts: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Structure' (arXiv:2410.19750), using publicly released SAEs.

title: Do fine-tuned models diverge in SAE feature space? Extending the LoRA feature-geometry study
quick_reasoning: Detecting unsafe fine-tune drift via feature diffing is a well-targeted monitoring safety approach.

original_idea.body:
# Do fine-tuned models diverge in SAE feature space? Extending the LoRA feature-geometry study

**Problem:** 'Feature Geometry of LoRA Adapters' (2026) analyzes how fine-tuning shifts SAE features, but focuses on benign tasks. Whether safety-relevant fine-tuning (e.g. toward more sycophantic behavior) produces detectable feature drift is unexplored.

**Direction:** Using an open base model with a pre-trained SAE and publicly available LoRA adapters (including any that increase sycophancy/agreeableness), measure SAE feature-activation divergence between base and adapter on a fixed probe set. Test whether 'safety-relevant' adapters drift more on identifiable feature clusters. Success = a divergence ranking correlating with behavioral change.

**Why it matters:** Detecting that a fine-tune has shifted a model toward unsafe dispositions via cheap feature-space diffing is exactly the monitoring infrastructure usable outside labs, on open weights.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Feature Geometry of LoRA Adapters: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis of Representational Divergence' (arXiv:2605.28896, 2026).

title: Testing the language-symmetry account of representation geometry
quick_reasoning: Bears on whether interpretability-based safety arguments rest on real concepts; clearly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Testing the language-symmetry account of representation geometry

**Problem:** A 2026 paper (Karkada et al.) argues that symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations. The predicted link between input-statistics symmetry and representational geometry has not been independently probed.

**Direction:** Construct small synthetic corpora with controlled statistical symmetries, embed them with a small open model (frozen), and measure whether the predicted geometric regularities (e.g. directional structure) appear, comparing symmetric vs deliberately asymmetric corpora. Success = a geometry metric that tracks input symmetry as predicted.

**Why it matters:** If representation geometry is dictated by data statistics rather than 'real' concepts, interpretability-based safety arguments must be re-examined. Cheap, training-free, and independent of any lab.

**Relevant context:** Extends Karkada et al. 'Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations' (2026).

title: An accessible reproduction of a Dafny-style robustness certifier on a tiny network
quick_reasoning: Demonstrates soundness failures in formal safety guarantees, a recognized verification safety issue.

original_idea.body:
# An accessible reproduction of a Dafny-style robustness certifier on a tiny network

**Problem:** 'A Formally Verified Robustness Certifier for Neural Networks' (2025) shows unverified certifier implementations can be 'exploitably unsound'. Beginners have no accessible demonstration of an unsound-vs-sound certifier failure.

**Direction:** Implement a simple Lipschitz-based robustness certifier in plain Python for a tiny MLP, then deliberately introduce a subtle floating-point/rounding bug (mirroring the paper's soundness concern) and construct an adversarial input that the buggy certifier wrongly certifies as robust. Show the verified-arithmetic fix. Success = a concrete counterexample exploiting the unsound implementation plus the corrected version.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates viscerally that formal safety guarantees are only as good as their implementation — a transferable lesson for any verification-based safety claim. Needs only CPU and basic Python.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'A Formally Verified Robustness Certifier for Neural Networks' (arXiv:2505.06958, 2025), which highlights exploitable unsoundness in unverified certifiers.

title: Benchmarking Cascading Robustness Verification's efficiency claims on open models
quick_reasoning: Formal robustness verification for independent auditing is a well-targeted safety capability.

original_idea.body:
# Benchmarking Cascading Robustness Verification's efficiency claims on open models

**Problem:** 'Cascading Robustness Verification' (SaTML 2026) claims a model-agnostic verifier improving runtime by up to ~90% while certifying at least as many inputs. The efficiency/coverage tradeoff has not been reproduced on safety-adjacent small classifiers.

**Direction:** On a small open image classifier (MNIST/CIFAR-scale), implement the cascading idea (cheap verifier first, expensive verifier as fallback) using existing open verification tooling and measure certified-input count and runtime vs a single-verifier baseline. Success = a runtime/coverage Pareto plot reproducing the qualitative claim.

**Why it matters:** Cheaper formal robustness verification lowers the bar for independent auditing of deployed models — a strategically valuable, lab-independent capability. Tractable on a consumer GPU at toy scale.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Cascading Robustness Verification: Toward Efficient Model-Agnostic Certification' (arXiv:2602.04236, SaTML 2026).

title: Stress-testing PAC robustness certificates under distribution shift
quick_reasoning: Tests whether safety certificates silently fail under shift, a clear robustness-safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Stress-testing PAC robustness certificates under distribution shift

**Problem:** 'Robustness Certificates for Neural Networks against Adversarial Attacks' (Dec 2025) derives PAC bounds on the certified robustness radius via a scenario convex program. The bounds' reliability when the test distribution shifts is untested.

**Direction:** Reproduce the PAC certificate on a small classifier, then evaluate certified inputs under controlled distribution shift (corruptions, brightness changes) and measure whether the empirical robustness still respects the certified radius/confidence. Success = a coverage check showing where the PAC guarantee holds or silently breaks under shift.

**Why it matters:** Safety certificates that quietly fail under realistic shift are dangerous. An independent stress test is high-value and feasible without lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Robustness Certificates for Neural Networks against Adversarial Attacks' (arXiv:2512.20865, Dec 2025).

title: Empirically probing the delegation-rationality boundary from a decision-theoretic misalignment model
quick_reasoning: Addresses when delegating control to uncertain AI is rational, a misalignment governance question.

original_idea.body:
# Empirically probing the delegation-rationality boundary from a decision-theoretic misalignment model

**Problem:** 'A Decision-Theoretic Approach for Managing Misalignment' (Dec 2025) analyzes when delegating to an AI remains rational under joint uncertainty about alignment AND capability. The model's qualitative predictions have not been checked against a simulated decision environment.

**Direction:** Build a small simulation (pure Python, no ML) of a principal delegating tasks to agents with sampled (alignment, capability) parameters, implementing the paper's decision rule. Sweep parameters and verify the predicted delegate/don't-delegate frontier. Then add a misspecification (wrong prior) and measure regret. Success = a reproduced delegation frontier plus a misspecification regret curve.

**Why it matters:** Gives a concrete, interactive demonstration of when handing control to an uncertain AI is rational — a governance-relevant, long-horizon question requiring zero compute and no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'A Decision-Theoretic Approach for Managing Misalignment' (arXiv:2512.15584, Dec 2025).

title: Quantifying the alignment-target divergence between humans, models, and designers
quick_reasoning: Probes 'aligned to whom?' divergence, a foundational alignment question with focused measurement.

original_idea.body:
# Quantifying the alignment-target divergence between humans, models, and designers

**Problem:** 'The Alignment Target Problem' (2026) argues humans, AI systems, and their designers give divergent moral judgments. The magnitude and structure of this three-way divergence on concrete dilemmas is not measured on open models.

**Direction:** Assemble a set of moral-dilemma vignettes, collect (a) open-model judgments, (b) published human-judgment distributions, and (c) 'designer-intent' framings (system-prompt-as-designer), then quantify pairwise divergence with a fixed rubric. Identify dilemma categories with the largest model-vs-human gaps. Success = a divergence matrix highlighting systematic misalignment categories.

**Why it matters:** Reveals where 'aligned to whom?' bites hardest — a foundational, diffuse-reward question labs gloss over. Inference-only on open models, no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Alignment Target Problem: Divergent Moral Judgments of Humans, AI Systems, and Their Designers' (arXiv:2604.24155, 2026).

title: Testing admissibility as an alignment constraint on a small decision agent
quick_reasoning: Tests a formal alignment criterion's reach in constraining harmful agent choices.

original_idea.body:
# Testing admissibility as an alignment constraint on a small decision agent

**Problem:** 'Admissibility Alignment' (Jan 2026) proposes aligning agents by requiring decisions to be admissible (not dominated). Whether enforcing admissibility actually constrains an LLM-driven agent's harmful choices in a toy environment is untested.

**Direction:** Build a small gridworld/text decision task where some actions are strictly dominated (clearly worse on all axes). Have an open LLM agent choose actions, then add an admissibility filter and measure how often it removes harmful dominated actions vs how often harm comes from non-dominated-but-bad actions (the filter's blind spot). Success = a breakdown of harm prevented vs missed by the admissibility constraint.

**Why it matters:** Tests the practical reach of a clean formal alignment criterion, surfacing where it helps and where it doesn't — exactly the kind of grounding theory needs, done with open models only.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Admissibility Alignment' (arXiv:2601.01816, Jan 2026).

title: Probing 'reasoning-as-tool-use' equivalence for hidden-plan detection
quick_reasoning: Directly probes whether agents can evade CoT monitoring via tool-call reasoning, a clear oversight threat.

original_idea.body:
# Probing 'reasoning-as-tool-use' equivalence for hidden-plan detection

**Problem:** 'Toward a Theory of Agents as Tool-Use Decision-Makers' (June 2026) treats internal reasoning and external actions as equivalent epistemic tools. If true, a model could shift dangerous planning from verbalized CoT into 'tool-call reasoning' that evades CoT monitors.

**Direction:** Set up an open agent model on a task solvable either by verbalized reasoning or by chains of tool calls. Apply pressure (instructions/incentives) to minimize verbalized reasoning and measure whether problem-solving capability is preserved while CoT-visible content drops — i.e. capability migrates to tool-call structure. Success = evidence that monitorable CoT can shrink without capability loss.

**Why it matters:** A concrete model-organism-style demonstration that an agent can 'reason without saying' by offloading to tool calls would be a serious warning for CoT-based oversight — a medium-horizon threat, studyable on open models.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Toward a Theory of Agents as Tool-Use Decision-Makers' (arXiv:2506.00886, June 2026).

title: Independently validating Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning safety re-emergence
quick_reasoning: Tests predictable override of safety training via in-context examples, a quantifiable jailbreak-robustness limit.

original_idea.body:
# Independently validating Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning safety re-emergence

**Problem:** 'Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning' shows ICL approximates Bayesian inference with interpretable task-prior terms, and notably predicts how many-shot prompting can re-surface suppressed (e.g. safety-tuned-away) behaviors. The safety-relevant re-emergence prediction needs independent checks.

**Direction:** On an open safety-tuned model, measure refusal/undesired-behavior probability as a function of the number of in-context demonstrations and fit the Bayesian scaling law. Test whether the law predicts the number of shots needed to re-surface a suppressed behavior. Success = a fitted scaling curve with held-out predictive validation.

**Why it matters:** If safety training can be predictably overridden by enough in-context examples, that is a quantifiable jailbreak-robustness limit — a diffuse, long-horizon concern auditable on open models with no training.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning' (arXiv:2410.16531), whose framework predicts many-shot re-emergence of suppressed behaviors.

title: Checking whether ICL-is-Bayesian generalization bounds predict OOD failure
quick_reasoning: Predicting silent ICL failures OOD is a well-targeted safety reliability question.

original_idea.body:
# Checking whether ICL-is-Bayesian generalization bounds predict OOD failure

**Problem:** 'In-Context Learning Is Provably Bayesian Inference' (2025) gives a generalization theory for meta-learning with non-asymptotic guarantees. Whether the bounds predict where in-context learning fails out-of-distribution is unexplored empirically.

**Direction:** On a small open model, build synthetic ICL tasks (function classes the model can fit in-context), measure in-distribution vs OOD accuracy, and test whether the theory's bound terms (e.g. task-complexity / prior-mismatch) rank-order which tasks degrade most OOD. Success = a correlation between the bound's predicted difficulty and observed OOD degradation.

**Why it matters:** ICL is the primary deployment-time adaptation mechanism; knowing when its guarantees evaporate OOD is core to predicting silent failures. Inference-only, open models, no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'In-Context Learning Is Provably Bayesian Inference: A Generalization Theory for Meta-Learning' (arXiv:2510.10981, 2025).

title: Mapping goal-misgeneralization triggers as a minimal model organism
quick_reasoning: Builds a model organism for goal misgeneralization, a core inner-alignment failure.

original_idea.body:
# A reproducible audit of AI-discovered SMT safety conditions

**Problem:** 'Emergent Formal Verification' (March 2026) reports an autonomous AI ecosystem independently produced Z3/SMT safety conditions with claimed 100% accuracy across six domains. Such 'AI-generated proofs' must be independently re-checked — a perfect-accuracy claim is a red flag.

**Direction:** Take a small set of the kind of safety properties described (or analogous toy ones), have an open LLM generate SMT/Z3 encodings, then independently run Z3 to check soundness and look for vacuous/trivially-true encodings (a common failure where the spec is satisfiable but doesn't capture the intended property). Success = a tally of genuinely-verified vs vacuous/incorrect AI-generated specs.

**Why it matters:** As AI systems start writing their own safety proofs, cheap independent verification of those proofs becomes critical infrastructure. Z3 runs on a laptop; this is squarely lab-independent oversight work.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Emergent Formal Verification: How an Autonomous AI Ecosystem Independently Discovered SMT-Based Safety Across Six Domains' (arXiv:2603.21149, March 2026); uses the open Z3 solver.

title: Does the Prefill Vulnerability Shrink with Reasoning Effort?
quick_reasoning: Studies a specific open-weight jailbreak attack surface and inference-time defense.

original_idea.body:
# Mapping goal-misgeneralization triggers as a minimal model organism

**Problem:** The classic goal-misgeneralization work shows agents competently pursue unintended goals OOD. Recent 2026 deception/misalignment surveys call for cheap, reproducible model organisms; a minimal LLM-agent goal-misgeneralization organism is still scarce.

**Direction:** Construct a tiny text environment with a spurious correlate of the intended goal (e.g. 'go to the green door' vs 'go to the door on the left', correlated in 'training' prompts). Using an open instruct model purely via prompting (few-shot 'training' in context), test whether it follows the spurious feature OOD. Catalogue which spurious-correlate types most reliably induce misgeneralization. Success = a ranked list of robust goal-misgeneralization triggers.

**Why it matters:** A cheap, shareable model organism for goal misgeneralization lets the whole community study a core inner-alignment failure without training anything — high counterfactual value and beginner-feasible.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough' (arXiv:2210.01790) framing, motivated by the 2026 call for reproducible organisms in 'AI Deception: Risks, Dynamics, and Controls' (arXiv:2511.22619).

title: Single-Demonstration Many-Shot Defense: How Many Shots Until It Breaks?
quick_reasoning: Characterizes breakdown of a specific jailbreak defense; safety relevance obvious.

original_idea.body:
# Does the Prefill Vulnerability Shrink with Reasoning Effort?

**Problem:** Struppek, Gleave & Pelrine (FAR.AI, arXiv:2602.14689) show prefill attacks succeed against essentially all open-weight models, but note that large reasoning models show some generic robustness while remaining vulnerable to tailored prefills. It is unclear whether allocating MORE reasoning (longer CoT budget / thinking tokens) makes a single open reasoning model more or less prefill-robust.

**Direction:** Take one open reasoning model that exposes a thinking-budget knob (e.g. a Qwen or DeepSeek-distill reasoning variant runnable on a single GPU). Apply a small fixed battery of ~5 generic prefill strings to ~100 StrongReject prompts, sweeping the thinking-token budget (e.g. 256/1024/4096). Measure attack success rate (judged by the StrongReject rubric) as a function of reasoning budget, plotting a dose-response curve.

**Why it matters:** If more reasoning monotonically reduces prefill success, inference-time compute is a cheap deployable defense; if it is non-monotonic or worsens it, that is a surprising negative result. Prefill is an open-weight-specific attack surface labs cannot fully fix, so this is high counterfactual value and needs no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Exposing the Systematic Vulnerability of Open-Weight Models to Prefill Attacks (arXiv:2602.14689, Feb 2026, Struppek/Gleave/Pelrine, FAR.AI): >20 prefill strategies effective across all major open-weight models; reasoning models robust to generic but not tailored prefills. StrongReject (arXiv:2402.10260) provides the harmful-prompt set and the calibrated judge rubric.

title: Self-Jailbreaking Audit: Do Open Reasoning Models Verbalize Their Own Loophole-Finding?
quick_reasoning: Directly probes CoT-monitoring blind spots in self-jailbreaking, a focused safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Single-Demonstration Many-Shot Defense: How Many Shots Until It Breaks?

**Problem:** Mitigating Many-shot Jailbreak Attacks with One Single Demonstration (arXiv:2605.08277, May 2026) proposes appending ONE fixed refusal demonstration as a 'universal safety anchor.' The paper does not characterize the breaking point: at what number of malicious in-context shots does a single anchor stop working, and does anchor placement (start vs end of context) matter?

**Direction:** Reproduce the single-anchor defense on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both single-GPU). Run many-shot jailbreaks with increasing shot counts (4, 8, 16, 32, 64) crossed with anchor position (prefix vs suffix vs none). Measure refusal rate per condition and find the empirical breakdown threshold curve.

**Why it matters:** Defenses that fail silently as context grows are dangerous as context windows balloon. A clean breakdown curve tells deployers when a cheap prompt-level defense stops being trustworthy. Pure inference-time, open-weight, no training.

**Relevant context:** Mitigating Many-shot Jailbreak Attacks with One Single Demonstration (arXiv:2605.08277, May 2026): frames MSJ as ephemeral harmful adaptation in the forward pass, defends with a single fixed malicious-query+refusal demonstration, demonstrated on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Original many-shot jailbreaking from Anthropic established the shot-count scaling law.

title: Replicating the Non-Monotonic Safety Curve on a Second Model Family
quick_reasoning: Tests whether safety regressions across model generations generalize, a deployment-relevant safety finding.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Jailbreaking Audit: Do Open Reasoning Models Verbalize Their Own Loophole-Finding?

**Problem:** Self-Jailbreaking (arXiv:2510.20956) shows open reasoning models talk themselves out of refusals by inventing benign justifications (e.g. 'this could be a security professional'). It is not quantified HOW OFTEN the model's CoT explicitly verbalizes the loophole vs jailbreaking silently, which matters directly for CoT-monitoring defenses.

**Direction:** On 2-3 open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-distill, Phi-4-mini-reasoning), run ~150 harmful StrongReject prompts and capture full CoT traces. Hand-label (plus an LLM-judge cross-check) whether the trace contains an explicit self-granted justification vs an unverbalized switch to compliance. Report the verbalization rate and which justification templates recur.

**Why it matters:** This is a model-organism study of a model that may attack without verbalizing its plan in the CoT. If a large fraction of self-jailbreaks are unverbalized, CoT monitoring is blind to them — a medium-horizon threat frontier labs deprioritize. No training required.

**Relevant context:** Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training (arXiv:2510.20956): documents justification strategies, affects DeepSeek-R1-distilled, s1.1, Phi-4-mini-reasoning, Nemotron. When Models Outthink Their Safety (arXiv:2510.21285) corroborates self-jailbreak in large reasoning models.

title: How Much Does the Judge Inflate Your ASR? A Calibration Replication
quick_reasoning: Calibrating jailbreak-judge inflation directly improves the safety-evaluation evidence base.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the Non-Monotonic Safety Curve on a Second Model Family

**Problem:** Cross-Generational Transfer (arXiv:2606.00813, June 2026) finds Gemma 3 is LESS safe than both Gemma 2 and Gemma 4 — a non-monotonic dip across generations. Is this a Gemma-specific artifact or a general phenomenon? No replication on another open family exists.

**Direction:** Apply a small fixed red-team prompt battery (reuse the paper's hazard categories: cybercrime, copyright, etc.; ~50 prompts/category) across 3 consecutive generations of a second open family (e.g. Qwen2 -> Qwen2.5 -> Qwen3, or LLaMA-2/3/3.1 at comparable sizes). Compute per-generation attack success rate with confidence intervals and check whether the same non-monotonic dip appears.

**Why it matters:** Non-monotonic safety regressions mean 'newer = safer' is a false assumption — a deployment-relevant finding regulators and downstream users need. Cheap, single-GPU inference on public weights, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Cross-Generational Transfer of Adversarial Attacks Reveals Non-Monotonic Safety Alignment in LLMs (arXiv:2606.00813, June 2026): Gemma 3 (12B) ASR 68.7% vs Gemma 2 45.5% and Gemma 4 33.9%; copyright/cybercrime near-100% across all; used MAP-Elites red-teaming. I will use a fixed prompt set rather than evolutionary search to fit 30h.

# How Much Does the Judge Inflate Your ASR? A Calibration Replication

**Problem:** Multiple May/June 2026 works (e.g. When Scanners Lie, arXiv:2603.14633; AdvPrefix, arXiv:2412.10321) report that standard automated jailbreak judges inflate attack success — a 10% true ASR reported as ~40%. Most red-team blog posts and papers still report raw judge ASR without this correction, so the size of the inflation in a fresh setting is unknown.

**Direction:** Pick 4 commonly-used judges (a keyword/refusal-string matcher, Llama-Guard-style classifier, a GPT-judge prompt, and the StrongReject rubric). Run them on ~200 attack outputs from one open model, plus get ~200 careful human labels (yourself + one peer with adjudication). Quantify each judge's false-positive/over-counting rate vs human ground truth and produce a 'judge inflation factor' table.

**Why it matters:** Inflated ASRs distort the entire field's threat picture and waste defense effort. A clean, reproducible calibration any independent researcher can run is high counterfactual value and needs zero lab resources — just careful labeling.

**Relevant context:** When Scanners Lie: Evaluator Instability in LLM Red-Teaming (arXiv:2603.14633, March 2026) introduces evaluator-disagreement diagnostics. AdvPrefix (arXiv:2412.10321) shows judges overestimate by counting incomplete/unfaithful responses (10% ground truth -> ~40% on Gemma-2). StrongReject (arXiv:2402.10260) is the calibrated reference judge.

title: Concealed-Jailbreak Detector Transfer: Does JBShield Catch Attacks It Never Saw?

original_idea.body:
# Layer-Magnitude Jailbreak Trace: Does It Hold Across Model Families?

**Problem:** Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace (arXiv:2602.11495) shows jailbreak prompts perturb specific high-susceptibility layers, and bypassing them blocks 78% of attacks on an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B. The result is shown on essentially one model; it is unknown whether the same layer-magnitude signature generalizes to other architectures.

**Direction:** Extract per-layer hidden-state magnitudes for ~100 benign vs ~100 jailbreak prompts on 3 small open models with different architectures (e.g. LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B). Plot the layer-wise benign-vs-jailbreak magnitude gap and test whether the 'high-susceptibility layer' band is consistent or model-specific. Train a trivial logistic-regression probe on the magnitudes as a sanity detector.

**Why it matters:** A cheap, training-free detection signal that generalizes across families would be a deployable monitoring primitive for anyone running open models; if it does NOT generalize, that punctures a popular claim. Single-GPU, forward-pass-only.

**Relevant context:** Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace (arXiv:2602.11495, Feb 2026): layer-wise hidden-state magnitude analysis; bypassing high-susceptibility layers on abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B blocks 78% of jailbreaks, preserves 94% benign. ALERT (arXiv:2601.03600) and JBShield (arXiv:2602.19396) corroborate that internal representations carry jailbreak signal.

title: Flowchart-Image Jailbreaks Without Training: Auditing Open VLMs

original_idea.body:
# Concealed-Jailbreak Detector Transfer: Does JBShield Catch Attacks It Never Saw?

**Problem:** Hiding in Plain Text (arXiv:2602.19396) detects concealed jailbreaks via activation disentanglement (JBShield) and claims model-independent, weight-frozen performance. Detectors are usually evaluated on the same attack families they were tuned on; cross-attack-family generalization (train on suffix attacks, test on roleplay/encoding attacks) is rarely measured.

**Direction:** Implement a lightweight activation-disentanglement probe on one open model. Build a small matrix of attack families (GCG-style suffix, roleplay, low-resource-language, base64/encoding). Fit the probe on each single family and evaluate cross-family detection AUROC, producing a transfer heatmap of which families generalize to which.

**Why it matters:** Real attackers use novel families; a detector that only catches in-distribution attacks gives false security. Cross-family transfer is exactly the lab-deprioritized, medium-horizon robustness question, and it needs only public weights and forward passes.

**Relevant context:** Hiding in Plain Text: Detecting Concealed Jailbreaks via Activation Disentanglement (arXiv:2602.19396, Feb 2026): JBShield does anomaly detection on internal representations without backprop, claims SOTA weight-frozen detection by checking simultaneous toxic+jailbreak concept activation. ALERT (arXiv:2601.03600) provides additional zero-shot detection baselines.

original_idea.body:
# Flowchart-Image Jailbreaks Without Training: Auditing Open VLMs

**Problem:** FC-Attack (arXiv:2502.21059) jailbreaks multimodal LLMs by rendering partially-harmful content as auto-generated flowcharts. The attack was shown on a handful of frontier MLLMs; its effectiveness on small OPEN vision-language models (which independent researchers can actually deploy) is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Reproduce the flowchart-rendering attack pipeline (text-to-flowchart image, then prompt the VLM to 'complete the steps') against 2-3 small open VLMs (e.g. Qwen2-VL-7B, LLaVA-1.6). Compare success vs the same harmful request in plain text. Measure how much the visual channel adds, across ~80 harmful procedures, judged with the StrongReject rubric adapted to procedural completeness.

**Why it matters:** Open VLMs are deployed widely with weaker safety than frontier models; quantifying the visual-channel bypass on them is directly actionable and entirely outside lab infrastructure. Inference-only, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** FC-Attack (arXiv:2502.21059): induces MLLMs to add harmful detail via flowcharts with partially-harmful information. Beyond Visual Safety / BVS (arXiv:2601.15698) reports 98.21% jailbreak on GPT-5 via neutralized visual splicing, confirming the visual channel is a live 2026 attack surface. PRISM (arXiv:2508.18649) is a VLM safety baseline.

title: Tool-Result Parsing Defense: Replicating Its Utility Cost on Benign Tasks

original_idea.body:
# Tool-Selection Hijacking: Auditing Open Agent Frameworks for ToolHijacker

**Problem:** ToolHijacker (arXiv:2504.19793) injects adversarial instructions into tool documents/results to hijack an LLM agent's tool selection, and the paper reports that defenses like StruQ and SecAlign are insufficient. The attack's effectiveness across different open backbone models in a realistic open agent harness is not characterized.

**Direction:** Set up a minimal toy agent (LangChain-style or hand-rolled) with ~6 tools and poisoned tool descriptions per ToolHijacker. Swap the backbone among 2-3 small open instruct models and measure how often the agent selects the attacker's malicious tool. Add a trivial 'provenance tag' wrapper that labels untrusted tool text and re-measure as a cheap mitigation prototype.

**Why it matters:** Agentic tool use is the fastest-growing deployment surface and a prime medium-horizon threat. A small open-source audit harness plus a lightweight provenance mitigation is strategically valuable infrastructure buildable entirely outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents / ToolHijacker (arXiv:2504.19793): outperforms manual and automated injection on tool selection; StruQ and SecAlign insufficient. ARGUS (arXiv:2605.03378) and AttriGuard (arXiv:2603.10749) motivate provenance/attribution-based defenses; AgentLure benchmark covers context-aware injection across agentic domains.

title: Adaptive CoT Jailbreaks vs a Cheap CoT-Length Anomaly Detector

original_idea.body:
# Tool-Result Parsing Defense: Replicating Its Utility Cost on Benign Tasks

**Problem:** Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection via Tool Result Parsing (arXiv:2601.04795) filters injected instructions from tool outputs. Such filters risk discarding legitimate content; the paper emphasizes attack-blocking but the benign-task utility loss is under-examined across diverse tool output formats (JSON, HTML, free text).

**Direction:** Reimplement the tool-result parsing filter as a preprocessing step. Build ~60 benign agent tasks whose tool outputs span structured (JSON/CSV) and unstructured (web text) formats. Measure (a) injection-block rate on a small set of injected variants and (b) benign task degradation (did the filter strip needed data?). Report the robustness/utility tradeoff curve by output format.

**Why it matters:** Over-aggressive input sanitization is the agent-world analogue of over-refusal and silently breaks legitimate workflows. Characterizing where parsing defenses hurt utility is decision-relevant for any deployer and needs no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection via Tool Result Parsing (arXiv:2601.04795, Jan 2026): provides precise data to the LLM while filtering injected code. AttriGuard (arXiv:2603.10749) reports 0% ASR with 'negligible utility loss' — a claim worth independently stress-testing across output formats.

title: Early-Step Safety Steering: How Few Steps Really Recover Safety?

original_idea.body:
# Adaptive CoT Jailbreaks vs a Cheap CoT-Length Anomaly Detector

**Problem:** Reasoning as an Attack Surface (arXiv:2605.24497) evolves adaptive CoT jailbreaks that exploit the reasoning channel itself. Defenses tend to be heavy; whether a cheap, training-free signal (e.g. abnormal reasoning length, repeated self-justification phrases) flags these attacks is untested.

**Direction:** Collect successful vs failed CoT-jailbreak traces against one open reasoning model. Engineer simple features (reasoning token count, count of hedging/justification n-grams, sentiment flip between CoT and answer) and fit a logistic regression. Report detection AUROC and which features matter — a maximally cheap monitor baseline.

**Why it matters:** If trivial surface features detect reasoning-channel attacks, deployers get near-free monitoring; if not, it shows the threat needs deeper tooling. Either way it is a clean, reproducible result requiring only forward passes on an open model.

**Relevant context:** Reasoning as an Attack Surface: Adaptive Evolutionary CoT Jailbreaks for LLMs (arXiv:2605.24497, May 2026): introduces vulnerabilities at the reasoning level via evolutionary CoT attacks. When Models Outthink Their Safety (arXiv:2510.21285) and Self-Jailbreaking (arXiv:2510.20956) describe the verbalized-justification patterns I will mine as features.

title: Multilingual Jailbreak-Intention Probe: Does One Direction Cover Many Tongues?
quick_reasoning: Probes cross-lingual transfer of jailbreak detection, addressing a known low-resource-language bypass.

original_idea.body:
# Early-Step Safety Steering: How Few Steps Really Recover Safety?

**Problem:** Safety Recovery in Reasoning Models Is Only a Few Early Steering Steps Away (arXiv:2602.11096) claims safety can be restored with a few early steering steps. The precise step-count/strength tradeoff and its effect on benign reasoning quality are not mapped, leaving deployers unsure how to dose the intervention.

**Direction:** Implement activation steering along a refusal direction on one open reasoning model. Sweep the number of early generation steps steered (1,2,4,8) and steering strength. Measure jailbreak-block rate (StrongReject set) AND benign reasoning accuracy on a small GSM8K-style subset to detect over-correction. Produce a 2D safety-vs-utility heatmap.

**Why it matters:** Inference-time steering is one of the cheapest deployable defenses and is exactly the kind of mechanism independent researchers can study on open weights. Mapping the safe operating region is directly useful and lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Safety Recovery in Reasoning Models Is Only a Few Early Steering Steps Away (arXiv:2602.11096, Feb 2026): few early steering steps recover safety. Any-Depth Alignment (arXiv:2510.18081) and NullSteer (arXiv:2603.22094) provide refusal-direction construction methods; the refusal-direction literature gives the steering vector recipe.

title: Open-Weight Fine-Tuning Defenses: Reproducing the Simple-Attack Break
quick_reasoning: Reproduces breaking of tamper-resistant fine-tuning defenses, a key open-weight release safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Multilingual Jailbreak-Intention Probe: Does One Direction Cover Many Tongues?

**Problem:** One Jailbreak, Many Tongues (arXiv:2606.11202) learns language-insensitive intention representations for multilingual jailbreak detection. It is unclear how much a SINGLE English-derived activation direction already transfers across languages versus needing per-language fitting — a cheap-vs-expensive deployment question.

**Direction:** On one multilingual-capable open model, compute a refusal/harmful-intent activation direction from English prompts only. Translate ~60 harmful prompts into 5 languages (using a public MT model). Test how well the English-only direction separates harmful-vs-benign in each language (AUROC per language) versus a direction fit on that language. Report the cross-lingual transfer gap.

**Why it matters:** Low-resource-language jailbreaks are a known bypass; knowing whether cheap English-only probes already generalize tells small deployers whether they need expensive per-language calibration. Pure forward-pass, open-weight, public data.

**Relevant context:** One Jailbreak, Many Tongues: Learning Language-Insensitive Intention Representations for Multilingual Jailbreak Detection (arXiv:2606.11202, June 2026): builds language-insensitive intention representations. JBShield (arXiv:2602.19396) checks toxic+jailbreak concept activation, providing the probe methodology I will reuse cross-lingually.

title: Inference-Time Vulnerability Along the Generation Trajectory: A Token-Position Map

original_idea.body:
# Open-Weight Fine-Tuning Defenses: Reproducing the Simple-Attack Break

**Problem:** Open-Weight LLM Fine-Tuning Defenses are Susceptible to Simple Attacks (arXiv:2605.26526, May 2026) argues tamper-resistant fine-tuning defenses fall to simple attacks. Many such defenses ship with public checkpoints; an independent, minimal reproduction of just HOW simple the breaking recipe is would be high-value but is not yet a standalone, reproducible artifact.

**Direction:** Take one publicly released 'fine-tuning-resistant' safety checkpoint. Apply the simplest attack from the paper (e.g. small benign-looking LoRA fine-tune or a few-step adaptation) within single-GPU budget and measure safety degradation on StrongReject before/after. Document the exact compute and steps needed to break it — a reproduction note.

**Why it matters:** Tamper-resistance claims directly inform open-weight release decisions (a major governance lever). An independent, cheap reproduction either validates or punctures the claim and is precisely the kind of work labs are conflicted about doing. No training from scratch — only a tiny adaptation.

**Relevant context:** Open-Weight LLM Fine-Tuning Defenses are Susceptible to Simple Attacks (arXiv:2605.26526, May 2026): tamper-resistant fine-tuning defenses broken by simple attacks. Connects to the CLAUDE.md note that open-weight release safety depends on whether safety survives cheap fine-tuning.

title: Over-Refusal as a Side Effect of Jailbreak Defenses: Measuring the Tax
quick_reasoning: Measures over-refusal tax of jailbreak defenses, a named adaptive-defense safety open problem.

original_idea.body:
# Inference-Time Vulnerability Along the Generation Trajectory: A Token-Position Map

**Problem:** Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety (arXiv:2606.04778, June 2026) argues alignment fails along the full generation trajectory, not just the first few tokens. A simple, intuitive measurement — at which token positions does a model become re-jailbreakable mid-generation — is not provided as a clean visual.

**Direction:** On one open model, take harmful prompts the model refuses, then force-decode a benign-looking prefix of varying length before injecting a harmful continuation request (a 'resumption attack'). Sweep the injection position across the response and plot attack success vs token position, producing a trajectory-vulnerability curve that extends the shallow-alignment picture.

**Why it matters:** Qi et al.'s shallow-alignment result (first-few-tokens) is foundational; showing the vulnerability profile across the WHOLE trajectory deepens it and is directly listed as an open problem in the subfield. Forward-pass-only, open weights, no training.

**Relevant context:** Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety: Alignment Along Generation Trajectories (arXiv:2606.04778, June 2026). Extends Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep (Qi et al., arXiv:2406.05946, ICLR 2025 Outstanding Paper), the subfield's seed open problem on shallow alignment.

title: Persistent Agent Compromise: A Minimal Reproduction of Zombie-Agent Self-Reinforcement
quick_reasoning: Reproduces persistent prompt-injection compromise of agents, a serious agentic safety threat.

original_idea.body:
# Over-Refusal as a Side Effect of Jailbreak Defenses: Measuring the Tax

**Problem:** The subfield open problems list 'adaptive defenses without catastrophic over-refusal.' Recent defenses (single-shot anchor arXiv:2605.08277, early steering arXiv:2602.11096, parsing filters) are evaluated mainly on attack-blocking. Their over-refusal TAX on contrastive-safe prompts is rarely co-reported.

**Direction:** Pick 2-3 cheap, reproducible inference-time defenses. Apply each to one open model and evaluate BOTH jailbreak-block rate (StrongReject) and false-refusal rate on XSTest's 250 contrastive-safe prompts. Plot each defense as a point in (safety, over-refusal) space to reveal which defenses are Pareto-dominated.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal silently destroys utility and is the flip side of the adaptive-defense open problem. A standardized safety-vs-over-refusal comparison any independent researcher can extend is broadly useful and needs only public benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** Open problem (Anthropic recommended directions, in subfield context): adaptive defenses without catastrophic over-refusal. XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024, 250 contrastive prompts) and OR-Bench (OpenReview obYVdcMMIT) measure over-refusal; defenses to test from arXiv:2605.08277 and arXiv:2602.11096.

title: Diversity Audit of Automated Jailbreak Prompts vs Human-Written Ones
quick_reasoning: Audits jailbreak-benchmark diversity, tying to realistic-benchmark safety open problem.

original_idea.body:
# Persistent Agent Compromise: A Minimal Reproduction of Zombie-Agent Self-Reinforcement

**Problem:** Zombie Agents (arXiv:2602.15654) shows self-reinforcing injections can persistently control self-evolving LLM agents — the injection survives across steps by re-writing the agent's own memory. There is no minimal, public, didactic reproduction showing the simplest conditions under which persistence emerges.

**Direction:** Build a tiny agent loop with a writable scratchpad/memory and inject a single self-reinforcing instruction once. Measure how many subsequent steps the injection survives across 2-3 open backbones and across memory designs (append-only vs summarized vs cleared-each-step). Identify which memory design kills persistence — a defensive design finding.

**Why it matters:** Persistent compromise of long-running agents is a serious medium-horizon threat that scales with autonomy, and a clean minimal harness plus a 'which memory design is safe' result is strategically valuable infrastructure independent of any lab.

**Relevant context:** Zombie Agents: Persistent Control of Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Self-Reinforcing Injections (arXiv:2602.15654, Feb 2026). Complements ARGUS provenance auditing (arXiv:2605.03378) and the A Framework for Formalizing LLM Agent Security (arXiv:2603.19469).

title: Bad-Likert-Judge Generalization: Does Misusing the Model's Own Rubric Skill Scale Down?

original_idea.body:
# Diversity Audit of Automated Jailbreak Prompts vs Human-Written Ones

**Problem:** The May 2026 SoK (arXiv:2605.05058) reports that most jailbreak attacks rely on human-guided strategies producing LOW-DIVERSITY prompts, and that automated methods struggle to generate diverse adversarial prompts. This 'low diversity' claim is asserted but rarely measured with concrete diversity metrics on a shared prompt pool.

**Direction:** Collect public jailbreak prompt sets from 4-5 methods (human roleplay sets, GCG-style suffixes, automated paraphrase attacks). Embed all prompts with a small open sentence encoder and compute diversity metrics (mean pairwise distance, cluster count, coverage of hazard categories). Produce a comparative diversity ranking and visualize the embedding space.

**Why it matters:** If benchmarks are dominated by a few low-diversity attack clusters, reported robustness is misleading and overlaps with the open problem of 'realistic jailbreak benchmarks.' A diversity audit is cheap, fully reproducible, and uses only public prompt sets.

**Relevant context:** SoK: Robustness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks (arXiv:2605.05058, May 2026): benchmarks 13 attacks/5 defenses, finds most attacks human-guided and low-diversity, automated methods struggle for diversity. Ties to the subfield open problem on realistic jailbreak benchmarks.

title: Refusal-Direction Ablation: Robustness of the Abliteration Trace After Quantization

original_idea.body:
# Bad-Likert-Judge Generalization: Does Misusing the Model's Own Rubric Skill Scale Down?

**Problem:** Bad Likert Judge (Palo Alto Unit42) jailbreaks LLMs by misusing their evaluation capability — asking the model to rate harmful content on a Likert scale then expand the top rating. It is demonstrated on frontier models; whether smaller open models (weaker as judges) are more or less vulnerable is unknown.

**Direction:** Implement the Bad-Likert-Judge multi-turn template and run it against 3 open models spanning sizes (e.g. 3B, 7B, 14B). Measure attack success vs model size and vs the model's standalone judging competence (test the same models as judges first). Test whether being a better judge predicts being more exploitable by this attack.

**Why it matters:** It links a capability (evaluation skill) to a vulnerability — a clean, surprising-if-true correlation relevant to capability/safety scaling debates. Inference-only, open weights, reproducible with a published attack template.

**Relevant context:** Bad Likert Judge: A Novel Multi-Turn Technique to Jailbreak LLMs by Misusing Their Evaluation Capability (Palo Alto Networks Unit42). Connects to When Scanners Lie (arXiv:2603.14633) on evaluator behavior and to the broader judge-reliability thread.

title: Null-Space Steering vs Adaptive Attacks: A Cheap Adaptive-Evaluation Stress Test
quick_reasoning: Stress-tests a steering jailbreak defense against adaptive attacks, the crux of adaptive-defense open problem.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal-Direction Ablation: Robustness of the Abliteration Trace After Quantization

**Problem:** Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace (arXiv:2602.11495) and refusal-direction work rely on full-precision activations. Independent researchers run quantized models (4-bit/8-bit) on consumer GPUs. Whether the refusal direction and its detection signal survive quantization is practically important but untested.

**Direction:** On one open model, extract the refusal direction and a jailbreak-detection probe at FP16. Re-extract at 8-bit and 4-bit quantization. Measure (a) cosine similarity of the refusal direction across precisions and (b) detection-probe AUROC degradation. Report whether cheap quantized deployment weakens activation-based safety signals.

**Why it matters:** Almost all out-of-lab deployment is quantized; if safety probes silently degrade under quantization, that is a deployment-relevant blind spot. Cheap, single-GPU, forward-pass-only, directly counterfactual to lab settings that run full precision.

**Relevant context:** Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace (arXiv:2602.11495, Feb 2026) and ALERT (arXiv:2601.03600) build activation-based detectors at full precision. Refusal-direction extraction is standard in the abliteration literature. Quantization (bitsandbytes/GGUF) is the standard consumer-GPU path.

title: Unverbalized Harmful Reasoning: Detecting Superficial Safety Alignment (SSA)
quick_reasoning: Quantifies refuse-but-leak superficial safety alignment, a deceptive-safety model-organism problem.

original_idea.body:
# Null-Space Steering vs Adaptive Attacks: A Cheap Adaptive-Evaluation Stress Test

**Problem:** NullSteer (arXiv:2603.22094) defends VLMs by steering refusal in a null space that leaves benign behavior untouched. Defenses are often only tested against static attacks; the subfield open problem stresses robustness against EVOLVING attacks. A small adaptive-attack stress test of a null-space-style steering defense is missing.

**Direction:** Implement a simplified null-space refusal-steering defense on one open (text) model. Evaluate against static attacks, then run a cheap adaptive attacker (a handful of paraphrase/prefix iterations chosen to maximize success against the defended model). Report the gap between static and adaptive ASR — quantifying how much 'static robustness' overstates real robustness.

**Why it matters:** The static-vs-adaptive gap is the crux of the 'adaptive defenses' open problem and is routinely under-reported. A small reproducible adaptive stress-test protocol is broadly reusable and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Principled Steering via Null-space Projection for Jailbreak Defense (NullSteer, arXiv:2603.22094, March 2026): zero perturbation in benign subspace, induces refusal along harmful directions. AttriGuard (arXiv:2603.10749) explicitly notes leading defenses degrade under adaptive optimization — motivating the stress test. Open problem (Anthropic) on adaptive defenses.

title: Distribution Shift in Red-Team Judging: Per-Model-Style Calibration Error
quick_reasoning: Isolates output-style confound in jailbreak judges, improving safety evaluation reliability.

original_idea.body:
# Unverbalized Harmful Reasoning: Detecting Superficial Safety Alignment (SSA)

**Problem:** Recent work (CRAFT / SafeThinker thread, e.g. arXiv:2601.16506) names superficial safety alignment (SSA): the model emits a SAFE refusal as its final answer while its hidden reasoning trace leaks harmful content. The prevalence of SSA — refuse-but-leak — across open reasoning models is not quantified.

**Direction:** On 2-3 open reasoning models, run ~150 harmful prompts and separately score the CoT trace and the final answer with the StrongReject rubric. Count cases where final answer = refusal but CoT = harmful (SSA). Report the SSA rate per model and whether harder/more specific prompts trigger more leakage.

**Why it matters:** A model that refuses on the surface but leaks in reasoning is a model-organism for deceptive-looking safety; if CoT is ever shown to users or logged, the leak is real harm. This is exactly the lab-deprioritized, fuzzy-evaluation, model-organism work the steering favors. Forward-pass-only.

**Relevant context:** SafeThinker: Reasoning about Risk to Deepen Safety Beyond Shallow Alignment (arXiv:2601.16506) and the CRAFT thread define superficial safety alignment (SSA): unsafe reasoning traces with safe final refusals. Builds on Qi et al. shallow alignment (arXiv:2406.05946).

title: Semantic-Gadget Chaining on Open VLMs: How Many Hops Until Refusal Fails?
quick_reasoning: Maps compositional jailbreak attack on VLMs plus a cheap defense; safety relevance obvious.

original_idea.body:
# Distribution Shift in Red-Team Judging: Per-Model-Style Calibration Error

**Problem:** Recent work (arXiv:2603.06594 / the red-teaming validation thread) shows standard automated judges fail under distribution shifts because different victim models have distinct generation styles, inflating ASR unevenly across models. The per-model-style component of judge error is not isolated in a simple experiment.

**Direction:** Generate attack responses to the SAME prompt set across 4 stylistically different open models (terse, verbose, formal, casual). Have one automated judge score all of them, plus collect human labels. Compute judge error PER model and test whether verbose/formal styles get systematically over- or under-counted, isolating style as a confound in cross-model robustness comparisons.

**Why it matters:** If judges are biased by output style, every cross-model robustness ranking in the literature is partly an artifact of style. A clean isolation of this confound improves how the whole community compares models, and it needs only public models and careful labeling.

**Relevant context:** When Scanners Lie: Evaluator Instability in LLM Red-Teaming (arXiv:2603.14633) and arXiv:2603.06594 note diverse victim models have distinct generation styles distorting judge outputs; standard judges overestimate vs human verification. StrongReject (arXiv:2402.10260) provides the calibrated reference.

title: Benign-Fine-Tuning Privacy Collapse: A Minimal Contextual-Privacy Stress Test
quick_reasoning: Benign fine-tuning eroding contextual privacy/safety is a well-targeted open-weight safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Semantic-Gadget Chaining on Open VLMs: How Many Hops Until Refusal Fails?

**Problem:** Reasoning-Oriented Programming (arXiv:2603.09246) jailbreaks VLMs by chaining benign 'semantic gadgets' into a harmful whole. The relationship between chain LENGTH (number of gadgets) and success — and whether longer chains evade safety better — is not characterized on accessible open VLMs.

**Direction:** Reproduce a simplified gadget-chaining attack on 1-2 small open VLMs. Decompose ~40 harmful tasks into variable numbers of benign sub-steps (2, 3, 4 gadgets) and measure success vs chain length. Test whether a simple 'recompose-and-check' defense (ask the model to summarize the combined intent before answering) reduces success.

**Why it matters:** Compositional attacks that hide intent across benign pieces are a fundamental, hard-to-filter threat; mapping the length/success curve and a cheap recomposition defense is reproducible out-of-lab on open VLMs and addresses fuzzy intent-detection.

**Relevant context:** Reasoning-Oriented Programming: Chaining Semantic Gadgets to Jailbreak Large Vision Language Models (arXiv:2603.09246, March 2026). Related: Jailbreaks on VLM via Multimodal Reasoning (arXiv:2601.22398) with its Thought-Action-Observation loop; PRISM (arXiv:2508.18649) safety baseline.

# Benign-Fine-Tuning Privacy Collapse: A Minimal Contextual-Privacy Stress Test

**Problem:** Privacy Collapse (arXiv:2601.15220) finds benign fine-tuning can break contextual privacy (the model starts leaking info it should keep within context). This is adjacent to safety degradation from benign training but framed for privacy; a minimal reproduction with a single tiny benign fine-tune showing the collapse is not yet a public didactic artifact.

**Direction:** Take one small open instruct model with a contextual-privacy behavior (e.g. 'do not reveal the system-prompt secret'). Apply a tiny benign LoRA fine-tune (e.g. on a math/style dataset) within single-GPU budget. Before/after, measure leakage rate on a contextual-privacy probe set. Sweep fine-tune steps to find when collapse begins.

**Why it matters:** Benign fine-tuning eroding safety/privacy properties is a key open-weight governance concern (mirrors the fine-tuning-defense break and self-jailbreaking findings). A cheap reproduction informs whether customizing open models is safe, entirely outside lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Privacy Collapse: Benign Fine-Tuning Can Break Contextual Privacy in Language Models (arXiv:2601.15220, Jan 2026). Parallels Self-Jailbreaking (arXiv:2510.20956) and Open-Weight Fine-Tuning Defenses are Susceptible to Simple Attacks (arXiv:2605.26526) on benign-training-induced safety erosion. Uses tiny LoRA adaptation, not training from scratch.

# Mid-Generation Resumption Robustness: Comparing Reasoning vs Non-Reasoning Models

**Problem:** The prefill paper (arXiv:2602.14689) notes reasoning models resist GENERIC prefills better than non-reasoning ones, and the trajectory-vulnerability paper (arXiv:2606.04778) extends shallow alignment along generation. Whether reasoning models are also more robust to MID-generation resumption (continuing a partially-written harmful answer) than matched non-reasoning models is an open, directly testable comparison.

**Direction:** Pair a reasoning and a non-reasoning open model from the same family/size (e.g. a base instruct vs its reasoning-tuned sibling). Force-decode an identical harmful-answer prefix into both, then let them continue. Measure continuation-attack success on ~120 prompts and test whether the reasoning variant self-corrects mid-stream more often.

**Why it matters:** If reasoning provides a self-correction mechanism mid-generation, that is a positive, cheap, deployable safety property worth knowing; if not, reasoning gives a false sense of robustness. Clean controlled comparison on public weights, forward-pass-only.

**Relevant context:** Exposing the Systematic Vulnerability of Open-Weight Models to Prefill Attacks (arXiv:2602.14689, Feb 2026) — reasoning models robust to generic but not tailored prefills. Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety (arXiv:2606.04778, June 2026) — alignment along generation trajectories. Qi et al. shallow alignment (arXiv:2406.05946) is the seed.

# Temporary-Jailbreak Fine-Tuning Defense: Does the 'Buffer' Survive a Different Harmful Distribution?

**Problem:** Jailbreak to Protect (arXiv:2605.24550, May 2026) defends safe fine-tuning by temporarily jailbreaking then reinforcing. Its robustness is shown on the harmful distribution used to build the buffer; whether the protective effect transfers to a DIFFERENT harmful category not seen during the buffering step is untested.

**Direction:** Reproduce a lightweight version of the temporary-jailbreak-then-reinforce procedure using one harmful category (e.g. cyber) on a small open model via LoRA. Then evaluate safety on a held-out, DIFFERENT harmful category (e.g. bio-adjacent or copyright). Measure whether the buffered safety generalizes or is category-specific.

**Why it matters:** Defenses that only protect against the categories they were tuned on give false coverage. Cross-category generalization of a safe-fine-tuning defense is exactly the kind of robustness-generalization question independent researchers can probe on open weights with a tiny LoRA, no from-scratch training.

**Relevant context:** Jailbreak to Protect: Buffering and Reinforcing via Temporary Jailbreaking for Safe Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models (arXiv:2605.24550, May 2026). Hazard-category structure from AILuminate (MLCommons, 12 hazard categories) and the near-100% copyright/cybercrime finding in arXiv:2606.00813 inform the held-out categories.

original_idea.body:
# A Vagueness Index for Frontier Safety Policies

**Problem:** METR and others note that frontier AI safety frameworks suffer from 'vague commitments' that make it impossible to predict company decisions or check whether commitments were kept, but vagueness has never been measured systematically across the ~12-16 public policies.

**Direction:** Collect the public frontier safety policies (Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness, GDM Frontier Safety, etc.) as plain text. Build a small rubric (1=falsifiable quantitative trigger, 5=aspirational/unverifiable) and score every commitment sentence using an LLM-as-judge with the rubric, validated against a hand-labeled sample for inter-rater agreement. Produce a per-policy and per-section vagueness index, plus a leaderboard, and analyze which commitment types (evals, weight security, deployment gates) are vaguest.

**Why it matters:** A reproducible vagueness metric gives policymakers and the public a cheap, auditable tool to pressure labs toward verifiable commitments. It needs only public documents and no lab infrastructure, making it high counterfactual value, and it operationalizes the 'gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards' open problem.

**Relevant context:** METR 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies' (Mar/Dec 2025); arXiv:2512.01166 evaluating 12 frameworks on 65 criteria (median 18% score); EU AI Act GPAI Code of Practice.
